newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Export strengths puts Australian trade in surplus.
newsitem.headline: Export strengths puts Australian trade in surplus.

text.p: Australia put in a better than expected trade performance in February, with strength in exports leading to the largest monthly surplus on goods and services since last July.

Official data released on Thursday showed a surplus of A$336 million on the balance of trade and services in February, a marked turnaround from January's A$38 million deficit, and well above median expectations of a small deficit in the month.
However, analysts warned that expected stronger growth in 1997 would most likely see a deterioration in the trade balance.
"Another trade surplus confirms a quite favourable performance, led by a steady improvement in exports," Citibank Australia senior economist Annette Beacher said.

Total exports of goods and services rose by 5.9 percent in the February, and the strength was spread across all components. Rural exports rose 4.8 percent, their fourth consecutive monthly rise, while non rural goods were up 7.1 percent and sevices exports rose 4.2 percent, their sixth consecutive monthly rise.

Imports were also up in the month, rising 1.5 percent, but not all categories rose. Service imports rose 1.9 percent and consumption and intermediate good imports were up 8.1 and 6.1 percent respectively, but capital goods fell 13.2 percent.
While capital goods are seen as an indicator of the level of business investment, the fall was not seen as concerning as it came after a massive 28.6 percent rise in January.
While exports outperformed imports in the month, the prospect of stronger growth further ahead in 1997 was a sign that import demand would pick up, with the trade position moving into deficit.
Not only were imports likely to pick up, but the recent strength in exports, particularly the rural sector was seen as unsustainable by economists.
"I can't see too much further upside in those numbers," HongKong Bank economist Anthony Thompson said.
For imports, stronger economic growth, a run down in inventory levels and capital expenditure increases would all be pointing to an increasing imports bill.
"So whilst it's good that the trend is continuing in surplus, I don't think it's going to be sustained throughout the whole year," Thompson said.
Markets are still adjusting to the new report, which only began two months ago when it replaced the monthly current account deficit, but already two key points were emerging.
One was a point that often got lost in the monthly current account deficit -- that Australia's external debt was not a function of its trade performance.
Bankers Trust chief economist Chris Caton said the data "should remind people that Australia does in fact sell as much to the rest of the world as we buy from it."
The second was that there was still great volatility in the monthly trade data, with the monthly balance changing by an average of A$360 million over the last four months.
"I think it just highlights that the goods and services balance is going to be just as hard to forecast as the monthly current account figures were," Commonwealth Bank economist Michael Blythe said.
